05-lists

Introduction

A list is a flexible R data structure that can contain multiple objects, including objects of different types.

Unlike a vector, which normally contains values of the same basic type, a list can contain:

  • Numbers
  • Character strings
  • Logical values
  • Vectors
  • Matrices
  • Other lists
  • Data frames
  • Functions
  • Other R objects

For example:

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE

This list contains a character value, a numeric value, and a logical value.

Key idea: A vector is usually homogeneous, while a list can contain heterogeneous objects.

Creating a List

Use the list() function.

my_list <- list(
  10,
  "Hello",
  TRUE
)

my_list
[[1]]
[1] 10

[[2]]
[1] "Hello"

[[3]]
[1] TRUE

The three elements have different types.

Check the type:

typeof(my_list)
[1] "list"

The result is:

list

Named Lists

It is usually more useful to give list elements names.

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE

The names can be retrieved using:

names(person)
[1] "name"    "age"     "student"

Accessing List Elements

There are three important ways to work with list elements:

$
[ ]
[[ ]]

Understanding the difference between them is essential.

Using [[ ]]

[[ ]] extracts the actual element from a list.

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person[[1]]
[1] "Sujan"

Access by name:

person[["name"]]
[1] "Sujan"

Access age:

person[["age"]]
[1] 25

The returned object is the actual value.

For example:

typeof(person[["age"]])
[1] "double"

Using $

The $ operator is commonly used with named lists.

person$name
[1] "Sujan"
person$age
[1] 25
person$student
[1] TRUE

This is equivalent to:

person[["name"]]
[1] "Sujan"
person[["age"]]
[1] 25
person[["student"]]
[1] TRUE

For named elements, these are usually interchangeable:

person$name
person[["name"]]

Tip: $ is convenient and readable, while [[ ]] is more flexible when the element name is stored in another variable.

Using [ ]

Single brackets select a sublist.

person[1]
$name
[1] "Sujan"

Compare:

person[1]
$name
[1] "Sujan"
person[[1]]
[1] "Sujan"

The first returns a list containing the first element.

The second returns the actual value.

This distinction is extremely important.

Example

person[1]
$name
[1] "Sujan"

returns a list.

person[[1]]
[1] "Sujan"

returns:

"Sujan"

[ ] vs [[ ]] vs $

Consider:

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)
Syntax Result
person[1] A list containing the first element
person[[1]] The first element
person["name"] A list containing name
person[["name"]] The value of name
person$name The value of name

A useful way to remember it:

[ ]       → subset of a list
[[ ]]     → extract an element
$         → extract a named element

Lists Can Contain Vectors

A list can contain vectors.

student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  scores = c(80, 90, 85)
)

student
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$scores
[1] 80 90 85

Access the vector:

student$scores
[1] 80 90 85

Then access an individual score:

student$scores[1]
[1] 80

This combines two indexing operations:

student
   ↓
$scores
   ↓
[1]

Lists Can Contain Matrices

A list can contain a matrix.

data <- list(
  name = "Scores",
  matrix = matrix(
    1:6,
    nrow = 2,
    byrow = TRUE
  )
)

data
$name
[1] "Scores"

$matrix
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

Access the matrix:

data$matrix
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

Access an element of the matrix:

data$matrix[1, 2]
[1] 2

Lists Can Contain Data Frames

Lists can also contain data frames.

student_data <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob"),
  score = c(85, 90)
)

student <- list(
  name = "Student Information",
  data = student_data
)

student$data
   name score
1 Alice    85
2   Bob    90

Nested Lists

Lists can contain other lists.

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  contact = list(
    email = "example@email.com",
    phone = "123456789"
  )
)

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$contact
$contact$email
[1] "example@email.com"

$contact$phone
[1] "123456789"

Access the nested list:

person$contact
$email
[1] "example@email.com"

$phone
[1] "123456789"

Access the email:

person$contact$email
[1] "example@email.com"

Or:

person[["contact"]][["email"]]
[1] "example@email.com"

Nested structures are common in real R objects.

Length of a List

Use length():

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

length(person)
[1] 3

This returns the number of top-level elements.

Structure of a List

Use str() to inspect the structure.

str(person)
List of 3
 $ name   : chr "Sujan"
 $ age    : num 25
 $ student: logi TRUE

str() is one of the most useful functions when working with complex R objects.

For example:

student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  scores = c(80, 90, 85),
  passed = TRUE
)

str(student)
List of 4
 $ name  : chr "Sujan"
 $ age   : num 25
 $ scores: num [1:3] 80 90 85
 $ passed: logi TRUE

It shows the names, types, and structure of the elements.

Tip: When you receive an unfamiliar R object, try str(object) first.

Modifying List Elements

You can modify an existing element.

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

person$age <- 26

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 26

Modify using [[ ]]:

person[["age"]] <- 27

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27

Adding New Elements

You can add an element using $.

person$country <- "Germany"

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27

$country
[1] "Germany"

Or:

person[["university"]] <- "TU Chemnitz"

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27

$country
[1] "Germany"

$university
[1] "TU Chemnitz"

Removing Elements

Assign NULL to remove a named list element.

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  country = "Germany"
)

person$country <- NULL

person
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

Check the result:

names(person)
[1] "name" "age"

Combining Lists

Use c() to combine lists.

list1 <- list(
  name = "Alice",
  age = 23
)

list2 <- list(
  city = "Chemnitz",
  student = TRUE
)

combined <- c(list1, list2)

combined
$name
[1] "Alice"

$age
[1] 23

$city
[1] "Chemnitz"

$student
[1] TRUE

Repeating Lists

Use rep() to repeat list elements.

x <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

rep(x, times = 2)
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

Converting a List to a Vector

If all elements are compatible, a list can sometimes be simplified into a vector.

x <- list(10, 20, 30)

unlist(x)
[1] 10 20 30

Result:

10 20 30

For a character list:

x <- list(
  "Alice",
  "Bob",
  "Charlie"
)

unlist(x)
[1] "Alice"   "Bob"     "Charlie"

Important: unlist() removes the list structure and attempts to create a simpler vector.

Named Lists and unlist()

Consider:

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

unlist(person)
   name     age 
"Sujan"    "25"

The result is a vector.

Because the vector must have a single basic type, R may perform type coercion.

Checking Whether an Object Is a List

Use:

is.list(person)
[1] TRUE

You can also use:

typeof(person)
[1] "list"
class(person)
[1] "list"

Lists and Vectors

A vector normally contains values of one basic type:

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30)

typeof(numbers)
[1] "double"

A list can contain different types:

mixed <- list(
  10,
  "Hello",
  TRUE,
  c(1, 2, 3)
)

mixed
[[1]]
[1] 10

[[2]]
[1] "Hello"

[[3]]
[1] TRUE

[[4]]
[1] 1 2 3

Compare:

Vector:
[10, 20, 30]

List:
[10, "Hello", TRUE, c(1, 2, 3)]

Lists and Matrices

A matrix has a fixed two-dimensional structure.

m <- matrix(
  1:6,
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

m
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

A list can contain multiple objects of completely different structures.

objects <- list(
  numbers = c(1, 2, 3),
  matrix = m,
  text = "Hello",
  flag = TRUE
)

objects
$numbers
[1] 1 2 3

$matrix
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

$text
[1] "Hello"

$flag
[1] TRUE

Lists and Data Frames

A data frame is closely related to a list.

Each column of a data frame can have a different type.

For example:

df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob"),
  age = c(23, 25),
  passed = c(TRUE, TRUE)
)

df
   name age passed
1 Alice  23   TRUE
2   Bob  25   TRUE

Conceptually, a data frame can be thought of as a collection of columns, where each column has the same number of rows.

You can inspect its structure:

str(df)
'data.frame':   2 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ name  : chr  "Alice" "Bob"
 $ age   : num  23 25
 $ passed: logi  TRUE TRUE

This relationship between lists and data frames will become important in the next chapter.

List Indexing — Important Examples

Consider:

student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  scores = c(80, 90, 85),
  passed = TRUE
)

First element

student[1]
$name
[1] "Sujan"

Returns a list.

First element’s value

student[[1]]
[1] "Sujan"

Returns the actual value.

Name

student$name
[1] "Sujan"

Name using [[ ]]

student[["name"]]
[1] "Sujan"

First score

student$scores[1]
[1] 80

All scores

student$scores
[1] 80 90 85

Second score

student[["scores"]][2]
[1] 90

Lists with Variables as Names

Suppose the element name is stored in a variable.

student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

field <- "name"

Using $:

student$field

This looks for an element literally named field.

Instead, use [[ ]]:

student[[field]]
[1] "Sujan"

This retrieves the element whose name is stored in field.

Important: [[ ]] is useful when the name or position is stored in a variable.

Useful List Functions

names()

Get or set names.

student <- list(
  "Sujan",
  25,
  TRUE
)

names(student) <- c(
  "name",
  "age",
  "student"
)

student
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE

length()

Get the number of top-level elements.

length(student)
[1] 3

str()

Inspect the structure.

str(student)
List of 3
 $ name   : chr "Sujan"
 $ age    : num 25
 $ student: logi TRUE

unlist()

Convert a list into a simpler vector when possible.

unlist(student)
   name     age student 
"Sujan"    "25"  "TRUE"

is.list()

Check whether an object is a list.

is.list(student)
[1] TRUE

Applying Functions to Lists

R provides several functions for applying operations to list elements.

One of the most useful is lapply().

numbers <- list(
  c(1, 2, 3),
  c(4, 5, 6),
  c(7, 8, 9)
)

lapply(numbers, mean)
[[1]]
[1] 2

[[2]]
[1] 5

[[3]]
[1] 8

This calculates the mean of each vector.

The result is another list.

sapply()

sapply() is similar to lapply() but tries to simplify the result.

sapply(numbers, mean)
[1] 2 5 8

The result may be a vector instead of a list.

Compare:

lapply(numbers, mean)
[[1]]
[1] 2

[[2]]
[1] 5

[[3]]
[1] 8
sapply(numbers, mean)
[1] 2 5 8

For beginners: Learn lapply() first. Later, sapply() and other apply-family functions can be explored in more detail.

List Function Reference

Function Purpose
list() Create a list
length() Number of top-level elements
names() Get or set element names
str() Inspect structure
is.list() Check whether object is a list
unlist() Simplify list into vector
c() Combine lists
rep() Repeat a list
lapply() Apply function and return list
sapply() Apply function and simplify result

List Indexing Reference

Given:

student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  scores = c(80, 90, 85)
)
Operation Code Result
First element as list student[1] List
First element student[[1]] Value
Name student$name Value
Name with [[ ]] student[["name"]] Value
Scores student$scores Vector
First score student$scores[1] Value
Scores with [[ ]] student[["scores"]] Vector
Second score student[["scores"]][2] Value

Python Comparison

If you know Python, a basic R list is somewhat similar to a Python list:

Operation R Python
Create list(1, "hello", TRUE) [1, "hello", True]
First element x[[1]] x[0]
Length length(x) len(x)
Add element x[[4]] <- value x.append(value)
Remove x[[2]] <- NULL del x[1]

However, R’s $ and named-list behavior makes R lists particularly useful for structured objects.

Practice Exercises

Exercise 1 — Create a List

Create a list called student containing:

  • Name
  • Age
  • University
  • A vector containing three exam scores
  • A logical value indicating whether the student passed

Then:

  1. Print the list.
  2. Print its structure using str().
  3. Print the student’s name.
  4. Print the second exam score.
  5. Print the number of elements.

Exercise 2 — Modify a List

Using your student list:

  1. Change the age.
  2. Add a country.
  3. Add another exam score.
  4. Remove the country.

Exercise 3 — Nested List

Create:

student
├── name
├── contact
│   ├── email
│   └── phone
└── scores

Then retrieve:

  1. Student name
  2. Email
  3. Phone
  4. First score

Exercise 4 — lapply()

Create:

numbers <- list(
  c(10, 20, 30),
  c(5, 15, 25),
  c(100, 200, 300)
)

Use lapply() to calculate:

  1. Mean
  2. Maximum
  3. Minimum

Then use sapply() and compare the results.

Key Takeaways

  • A list can contain objects of different types.
  • Lists can contain vectors, matrices, data frames, and other lists.
  • list() creates a list.
  • $ accesses a named element.
  • [[ ]] extracts an individual element.
  • [ ] returns a sublist.
  • Understanding [ ], [[ ]], and $ is essential when working with lists.
  • Lists can be nested.
  • str() is extremely useful for understanding complex objects.
  • unlist() can simplify a list into a vector.
  • lapply() applies a function to each list element and returns a list.
  • Data frames are closely related to lists, which will become clearer in the next chapter.
